title: Kindness is the altar (Avot de-Rabbi Natan 4)
hookLine: at the ruined Temple, Yochanan ben Zakkai teaches: we have kindness, as it is written "I desire mercy" (Hosea 6:6)
tomorrow: what happens when Moses sits in on a class about Moses?

cards: When a place that mattered closes, the old diner, the summer camp, a grandparent's house, the ride home usually has two voices in it. One says: it's gone, and it's right to be wrecked about it.

The other says: what made it matter is still here, in us. In a collection called Avot de-Rabbi Natan, two sages walk out of Jerusalem and have that exact argument, over a far larger loss. The Temple is in ruins.

teach.h: WOE TO US: THE ALTAR IS GONE.
teach.b: Rabbi Joshua looks at the rubble and says: woe to us. This was the place where Israel's wrongs were atoned for, and it's destroyed. His teacher, Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, answers: my son, don't grieve.
We have another atonement just as strong. Acts of loving-kindness, gemilut chasadim.
And he quotes Hosea: "For I desire mercy, and not sacrifice." Now let each one make his case, because the tradition kept both.

Rabbi Joshua: something holy really is gone. The altar was where a person could bring a wrong and set it down. Pretending that doesn't matter would be a lie, and Jewish life still mourns the Temple on Tisha b'Av.
Rabban Yochanan: if atonement lived only in a building, it would have died with the building. But the prophet already said what God wants: mercy.

teach.h: THE ALTAR MOVES TO THE TABLE.
teach.b: So the altar moves, into kitchens and hospital rooms, a meal carried to a house of mourning.
The Talmud even says loving-kindness is wider than charity: it can be done with your hands and your time, for rich and poor alike.
One to tell a friend tonight: Pirkei Avot says the world stands on three things, and acts of loving-kindness is one of them. Neither sage loses this argument. Grief says the loss was real.
Kindness says the work goes on.

how: Jewish life names gemilut chasadim, acts of loving-kindness, among the pillars of the world: visiting the sick, bringing meals to mourners, lending without interest, and attending weddings and funerals. The Temple is still mourned on Tisha b'Av.

games.q: what does “kindness is the altar” mean?
o: acts of loving-kindness, as strong as the old altar
a vow to rebuild the Temple through charity alone
a new altar built from the Temple's fallen stones

games.q: two sages in the ruins — tap the pairs.
p: woe to us: the place of atonement is gone
we have kindness, just as strong
I desire mercy, and not sacrifice
the day the Temple is still mourned

s: once kindness replaced the altar, Judaism stopped mourning the Temple
the tradition kept both: the Temple is still mourned on Tisha b'Av.
Rabban Yochanan answers the ruins by quoting Hosea
"For I desire mercy, and not sacrifice."
loving-kindness just means giving money to the poor
the Talmud calls it wider than charity: hands and time, for rich and poor.

games.q: your mom says, "don't mourn the house. it's just a house." you disagree. what's the strongest version of her side?
o: what made the house matter, the kindness in it, never needed the building.
a house is only money, and money shouldn't make anyone sad.
being sad wastes time when there are boxes to pack.
games.why: that's Rabban Yochanan's best case: the altar moves into acts of kindness. and Rabbi Joshua's grief is real too; the tradition kept both.

practice: Choose one person who could use a small kindness today. Write them a text that gives instead of asks: a thank-you, an offer of help, a memory of them at their best.
Send it now, or set it ready to send, and let it be today's offering.

wordCard.voice: Kindness is the altar: Rabban Yochanan's answer in the ruins. Acts of loving-kindness atone as the altar did, because God desires mercy.

orig.note: Hebrew: acts of loving-kindness, Rabban Yochanan's atonement after the Temple.

carryVoice: Kindness is the new altar, and any table can hold one. Thirty-two in, eight to go.

sources.ref: Avot de-Rabbi Natan (version A) 4 (Rabbi Joshua: woe to us; Rabban Yochanan: we have another atonement, gemilut chasadim)

sources.q: For I desire mercy, and not sacrifice

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Sukkah 49b (loving-kindness is greater than charity: with body and money, to rich and poor)
Pirkei Avot 1:2 (the world stands on Torah, service and acts of loving-kindness)
